{{short description|Allele equilibrium in a population when creation equals elimination by negative selection}}
'''Mutation–selection balance''' is an equilibrium in the number of deleterious [[allele]]s in a population that occurs when the rate at which deleterious alleles are created by [[mutation]] equals the rate at which deleterious alleles are eliminated by [[Natural selection|selection]].<ref name="auto">{{cite book|first1=James F.|last1=Crow|first2=Motoo|last2=Kimura|title=An Introduction to Population Genetics Theory|date=1970|publisher=Blackburn Press|location=New Jersey|isbn=9781932846126|edition=[Reprint]}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lynch|first1=Michael|title=Evolution of the mutation rate|journal=Trends in Genetics|date=August 2010|volume=26|issue=8|pages=345–352|doi=10.1016/j.tig.2010.05.003|pmid=20594608|pmc=2910838}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{cite book|last1=Barton|first1=Nicholas H.|title=Evolution|date=2007|publisher=Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press|location=Cold Spring Harbor, NY|isbn=9780879696849}}</ref><ref name="auto2">Herron, JC and S Freeman. 2014. Evolutionary Analysis, 5th Edition. Pearson.</ref> The majority of genetic mutations are neutral or deleterious; beneficial mutations are relatively rare. The resulting influx of deleterious mutations into a population over time is counteracted by [[Negative selection (natural selection)|negative selection]], which acts to purge deleterious mutations. Setting aside other factors (e.g., [[balancing selection]], and [[genetic drift]]), the equilibrium number of deleterious alleles is then determined by a balance between the deleterious mutation rate and the rate at which selection purges those mutations.

Mutation–selection balance was originally proposed to explain how [[genetic variation]] is maintained in populations, although several other ways for deleterious mutations to persist are now recognized, notably [[balancing selection]].<ref name="auto1"/> Nevertheless, the concept is still widely used in [[evolutionary genetics]], e.g. to explain the persistence of deleterious alleles as in the case of [[spinal muscular atrophy]],<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1086/301608 | volume=61 | issue=5 | title=De Novo Rearrangements Found in 2% of Index Patients with Spinal Muscular Atrophy: Mutational Mechanisms, Parental Origin, Mutation Rate, and Implications for Genetic Counseling | journal=The American Journal of Human Genetics | pages=1102–1111 | pmid=9345102 | pmc=1716038 | last1 = Wirth | first1 = B | last2 = Schmidt | first2 = T | last3 = Hahnen | first3 = E | last4 = Rudnik-Schöneborn | first4 = S | last5 = Krawczak | first5 = M | last6 = Müller-Myhsok | first6 = B | last7 = Schönling | first7 = J | last8 = Zerres | first8 = K| year=1997 }}</ref><ref name="auto2"/> or, in theoretical models, mutation-selection balance can appear in a variety of ways and has even been applied to beneficial mutations (i.e. balance between selective loss of variation and creation of variation by beneficial mutations).<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Beneficial Mutation–Selection Balance and the Effect of Linkage on Positive Selection|first1=Daniel S.|last1=Fisher|first2=Michael M.|last2=Desai|date=July 1, 2007|journal=Genetics|volume=176|issue=3|pages=1759–1798|doi=10.1534/genetics.106.067678|pmid=17483432|pmc=1931526}}</ref>

==Haploid population==

As a simple example of mutation-selection balance, consider a single [[gene locus|locus]] in a [[haploid]] population with two possible alleles: a normal allele ''A'' with [[allele frequency|frequency]] <math> p </math>, and a mutated deleterious allele ''B'' with frequency <math> q </math>, which has a small relative [[Fitness (biology)|fitness]] disadvantage of <math>s</math>. Suppose that deleterious mutations from ''A'' to ''B'' occur at rate <math> \mu </math>, and the reverse beneficial mutation from ''B'' to ''A'' occurs rarely enough to be negligible (e.g. because the mutation rate is so low that <math>q</math> is small). Then, each generation selection eliminates deleterious mutants reducing <math> q </math> by an amount <math>spq</math>, while mutation creates more deleterious alleles increasing <math> q </math> by an amount <math> \mu p </math>. Mutation–selection balance occurs when these forces cancel and <math> q </math> is constant from generation to generation, implying <math> q = \mu/s </math>.<ref name="auto1"/> Thus, provided that the mutant allele is not weakly deleterious (very small <math>s</math>) and the mutation rate is not very high, the equilibrium frequency of the deleterious allele will be small.

==Diploid population==

In a [[diploid]] population, a deleterious allele ''B'' may have different effects on individual fitness in heterozygotes ''AB'' and homozygotes ''BB'' depending on the degree of dominance of the normal allele ''A''. To represent this mathematically, let the relative fitness of deleterious [[homozygotes]] and [[heterozygotes]] be smaller than that of normal homozygotes ''AA'' by factors of <math>1-hs</math> and <math>1-s</math> respectively, where <math>h</math> is a number between <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> measuring the degree of dominance (<math>h=0</math> indicates that ''A'' is completely dominant while <math>h=1/2</math> indicates no dominance). For simplicity, suppose that [[Hardy–Weinberg principle|mating is random]].

The degree of dominance affects the relative importance of selection on heterozygotes versus homozygotes. If ''A'' is not completely dominant (i.e. <math>h</math> is not close to zero), then deleterious mutations are primarily removed by selection on heterozygotes because heterozygotes contain the vast majority of deleterious ''B'' alleles (assuming that the deleterious mutation rate <math>\mu</math> is not very large). This case is approximately equivalent to the preceding haploid case, where mutation converts normal homozygotes to heterozygotes at rate <math>\mu</math> and selection acts on heterozygotes with selection coefficient <math>hs</math>; thus <math>q\approx\mu/hs</math>.<ref name="auto"/>

In the case of complete dominance (<math>h=0</math>), deleterious alleles are only removed by selection on ''BB'' homozygotes. Let <math>p_{AA}</math>, <math>2 p_{AB}</math> and <math>p_{BB}</math> be the frequencies of the corresponding [[genotype]]s. The frequency <math>p=p_{AA}+p_{AB}</math> of normal alleles ''A'' increases at rate <math>1/(1-s p_{BB})</math> due to the selective elimination of recessive homozygotes, while mutation causes <math>p</math> to decrease at rate <math>1-\mu</math> (ignoring [[Back-mutation|back mutations]]). Mutation–selection balance then gives <math>p_{BB}=\mu/s</math>, and so the frequency of deleterious alleles is <math>q=\sqrt{\mu/s}</math>.<ref name="auto"/> This equilibrium frequency is potentially substantially larger than for the case of partial dominance, because a large number of mutant alleles are carried in heterozygotes and are shielded from selection.

Many properties of a non random mating population can be explained by a random mating population whose [[effective population size]] is adjusted. However, in non-steady state [[population dynamics]] there can be a lower prevalence for recessive disorders in a random mating population during and after a growth phase.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=La Rocca|first1=Luis A.|last2=Frank|first2=Julia|last3=Bentzen|first3=Heidi Beate|last4=Pantel|first4=Jean-Tori|last5=Gerischer|first5=Konrad|last6=Bovier|first6=Anton|last7=Krawitz|first7=Peter M.|date=2020-12-22|title=A lower prevalence for recessive disorders in a random mating population is a transient phenomenon during and after a growth phase|class=q-bio.PE|eprint=2012.04968}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=7 June 2020|title=visualization of effects of different mating schemes|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hOgLyRqWPg|website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>

==Multilocus mutation-selection balance==

Several studies have extended mutation-selection balance to whole-genome models.<ref name="K&M1966">{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=Motoo |last2=Maruyama |first2=Takeo |title=The Mutational Load with Epistatic Gene Interactions in Fitness |journal=Genetics |date=6 December 1966 |volume=54 |issue=6 |pages=1337–1351 |doi=10.1093/genetics/54.6.1337 |pmid=17248359 }}</ref><ref name="K1995">{{cite journal |last1=Kondrashov |first1=Alexey S. |title=Dynamics of unconditionally deleterious mutations: Gaussian approximation and soft selection |journal=Genetical Research |date=April 1995 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=113–121 |doi=10.1017/s0016672300033139 |pmid=7605513 }}</ref><ref name="R1998">{{cite journal |last1=Rice |first1=WR |title=Requisite mutational load, pathway epistasis and deterministic mutation accumulation in sexual versus asexual populations. |journal=Genetica |date=1998 |volume=102-103 |issue=1–6 |pages=71–81 |doi=10.1023/A:1017055429755 |pmid=9766966}}</ref><ref name="Ch1990">{{cite journal |last1=Charlesworth |first1=Brian |title=Mutation-selection balance and the evolutionary advantage of sex and recombination |journal=Genetical Research |date=June 1990 |volume=55 |issue=3 |pages=199–221 |doi=10.1017/s0016672300025532 |pmid=2394378 }}</ref><ref name="B&B2003">{{cite journal |last1=Baake |first1=Michael |last2=Baake |first2=Ellen |title=An Exactly Solved Model for Mutation, Recombination and Selection |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |date=1 February 2003 |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=3–41 |doi=10.4153/CJM-2003-001-0|arxiv=math/0210422 }}</ref><ref name="H1978">{{cite journal |last1=Haigh |first1=John |title=The accumulation of deleterious genes in a population—Muller's Ratchet |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |date=October 1978 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=251–267 |doi=10.1016/0040-5809(78)90027-8 |bibcode=1978TPBio..14..251H }}</ref>

For asexual organisms, let all mutations have the same multiplicative effect on fitness, that is the relative fitness of an individual with <math>k</math> segregating mutations is <math>w_i = (1-s)^k</math>. At mutation-selection balance, the probability that an individual has <math>k</math> segregating mutations follows a [[Poisson distribution]] with mean <math>\frac{U_d}{s_d}</math> where <math>U_d</math> is the whole genome deleterious mutation rate.<ref name="H1978"/>

For sexual organisms, models also have to consider recombination. If all mutations have the same additive effect on Malthusian fitness, the fitness of an individual is <math>w_i = e^{-sk}</math> where k is the number of mutations that an individual carries. Under this model the expected number of segregating deleterious mutations per individual is <ref name="K1995"/>

<math>
\bar{k}=\frac{U_d}{s_d}</math>.

In the limit of weak selection <math>w_i = e^{-sk} \approx (1-s)^k</math>.

==Mutation-selection-drift balance==

Mutation–selection balance models assume that the frequency of a deleterious allele is fixed (<math>\frac{q}{\mu}</math>). This ignores stochastic fluctuations in allele frequency due to genetic drift.

A popular approach is to use the diffusion approximation to compute the probability distribution of allele frequency <math>q</math> with a given selection coefficient <math>s</math>. Mathematically, this is represented by <math>P(q|s)</math>. This approach yields <ref name="Wright19">{{cite journal | last=Wright | first=Sewall | title=The Distribution of Gene Frequencies in Populations | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=23 | issue=6 | date=1937 | issn=0027-8424 | pmid=16577780 | pmc=1076930 | doi=10.1073/pnas.23.6.307 | pages=307–320 | url=https://pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.23.6.307 | access-date=2026-07-09}}</ref>

<math>P(q|s)=C(s)e^{4Nsq}q^{4N\mu_d-1}(1-q)^{4N\mu_r-1}</math>

where <math>N</math> is the population size, <math>\mu_d</math> and <math>\mu_r</math> are the deleterious and reverse mutation rate, and C(s) is the [[normalizing constant]]

<math>\int_0^{1}{e^{4Nsq}q^{4N\mu_d-1}(1-q)^{4N\mu_r-1}dq}</math>

Although this approximation works for common allele frequencies, rare alleles close to the 
<math>q=0</math> or <math>q=1</math> boundaries are not well characterized by this approach.<ref name="Ewens2024_Ch5">{{cite book | last=Ewens | first=Warren J. | title=Mathematical Population Genetics | chapter=Applications of Diffusion Theory | publisher=Springer New York | publication-place=New York, NY | volume=27 | date=2004 | isbn=978-1-4419-1898-7 | doi=10.1007/978-0-387-21822-9_5 | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-0-387-21822-9_5 | access-date=2026-07-09 | pages=156–200}}</ref>

==Epistasis and mutation-selection balance==

Mutation–selection balance is affected by [[epistasis]]. Epistasis means that the effect on fitness of a mutation is conditional on the presence of other mutations. Negative epistasis occurs when the decrease on fitness of a group of mutations is greater than expected by their individual contribution.

The strongest form of negative epistasis is threshold selection. In this selection regime the fitness of an individual is one below a number of segregating mutations but drops to zero beyond such number. Under this selection regime, the mean number of segregating mutations per individual at mutation-selection balance is

<math>
\bar{k}=\frac{U_d}{\delta}(2-\rho)</math>

where <math>\delta</math> is the selection differential divided by the variance on the distribution of segregating mutations and <math>
\rho</math> is the ratio of variances of the trait before and after selection.<ref name="K1995"/>

== Example ==
The first paper on the subject was ([[J. B. S. Haldane|Haldane]], 1935), which used the prevalence and fertility ratio of [[haemophilia]] in males to estimate mutation rate in human genes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Haldane |first=J. B. S. |date=October 1935 |title=The rate of spontaneous mutation of a human gene |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf02982403 |journal=Journal of Genetics |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=317–326 |doi=10.1007/bf02982403 |issn=0022-1333|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>Nachman, Michael W. "Haldane and the first estimates of the human mutation rate." ''Journal of Genetics'' 83 (2004): 231-233.</ref>

The prevalence of hemophilia among males is <math>p \in [4, 17] \times 10^{-5}</math>. The fertility ratio of males with hemophilia to males without hemophilia is <math>f \in [0.1, 0.25]</math>, where <math>f = \frac{\#(\text{offsprings of abnormal allele)}}{\#(\text{offsprings of normal allele)}} 
</math>.

Assuming hemophilia is purely due to mutations on the [[X chromosome]], the mutation rate can be estimated as follows.

At mutation-selection balance, the rate of new hemophilia cases due to mutations should be equal to the rate of hemophilia cases lost due to the lower fitness of hemophilia patients. Since every male has one X chromosome, the rate of new hemophilia cases due to mutations is <math>\mu</math>. On the other hand, the relative fitness of hemophilia patients is <math>f</math>, so <math>(1-f)</math> times the existing hemophilia cases are lost every generation due to selection. The mutation-selection balance thus gives 
<math display="block">
\mu = (1-f) p.
</math>
However, since females have two X chromosomes, only about 1/3 of the new mutations would appear in males (assuming an equal [[Human sex ratio|sex ratio]] at birth). Thus, the equation 
<math display="block">
\mu \approx (1-f)p/3 \in [1, 5] \times 10^{-5},
</math>
is obtained, where the numerical range was obtained by plugging in the ranges for <math>p</math> and <math>f</math>. Subsequent research using different methods showed that the mutation rate in many genes is indeed on the order of <math>10^{-5}</math> per generation.
